passage:
Monday, a cold December morning at the crèche. Alka pushed away the bowl of mashed sweet potato. 'No!'

Wednesday. Lavanya sat beside her, scooping orange mash into her mouth and humming, smearing it on her cheeks. Alka watched the spoon go up and down. She touched the mash with one finger.

Friday. Lavanya said, 'Yum!' and opened her mouth wide. Alka picked up her own spoon, took a tiny bite, then another, and banged the bowl for more.

qa.q: What food did Alka push away on Monday?
qa.a: The bowl of mashed sweet potato.

qa.q: What does Alka touching the mash with one finger on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was curious but still cautious, starting to trust the food after watching Lavanya enjoy it.

qa.q: How could the crèche staff help a child try a new food?
qa.a: They could seat the child beside a friend who enjoys the food and let the child watch, without forcing a bite.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had made a face at the sweet potato?
qa.a: Alka would probably have stayed wary and kept pushing the bowl away, since Lavanya's enjoyment was what signalled it was safe.

grounding: A toddler tries a new food only after watching another child eat it happily over several days.

passage: In the Ludhiana flat, Mehak sat in her high chair, lips shut tight against the spoon of dal-khichdi. Mummy sighed. Then cousin Himani, four, climbed onto the chair opposite with her own bowl. 'Mmm! Khichdi!' She ate a big spoonful, swinging her legs. Mehak stared. Himani ate another. Mehak opened her mouth, and Mummy slipped the spoon in. Mehak chewed, then pointed at both bowls, grinning. Himani clapped. 'She likes it like me!'

qa.q: What was on the spoon Mehak refused?
qa.a: Dal-khichdi.

qa.q: Why did Mehak open her mouth after watching Himani?
qa.a: Seeing Himani eat happily made the khichdi seem safe and good, so Mehak felt trusting and curious enough to try.

qa.q: What could Mummy try at the next meal with a new food?
qa.a: She could seat Mehak near Himani or another child who enjoys the food, so Mehak can watch before tasting.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Mehak started eating?
qa.a: Himani felt proud and delighted, clapping and saying Mehak likes it just like her.

grounding: A toddler refuses a food until she sees her cousin eat it happily, then tries it herself.

passage:
'Swati, try the mango, baby.'
'No-no.' Swati turned her face away.
'She won't,' said her brother Arjun. 'She never eats new stuff.'
Next door's Shalini toddled over. 'Mango!' She grabbed a slice and sucked it noisily, juice down her chin.
Swati watched. 'Mango?'
'Yes, mango,' said Amma.
Swati took a slice, licked it, then bit. 'Mmm!'
Arjun's mouth fell open. 'Amma, I tried for a week!'
Amma laughed. 'She needed to see a friend do it.'

qa.q: Who grabbed a mango slice first?
qa.a: Next door's Shalini grabbed a slice and sucked it noisily.

qa.q: What made Swati willing to try the mango?
qa.a: Watching Shalini enjoy it made the mango seem safe, so Swati felt curious and brave enough to lick and bite a slice.

qa.q: What could Amma do next time Swati refuses a new food?
qa.a: Amma could invite Shalini or another child to eat it nearby, letting Swati watch first.

qa.q: How does Arjun feel when Swati finally eats the mango?
qa.a: Arjun is surprised and a little frustrated, since his week of trying failed where one friend's example worked.

grounding: A toddler tries mango only after watching another child eat it happily, while her brother reacts in surprise.

passage:
Class teacher's note to Shankar's parents, after the monsoon break

Shankar seemed unsettled this week. Since school reopened, about fifteen children have come with the same blue astronaut bag. On Tuesday Shankar kept his old bag under the desk instead of on the hook. On Wednesday he asked me, 'Everyone has it, so it must be the best one, no?' When I asked what he liked about it, he thought, then said, 'The zip? I don't know. Everyone has it.' His own bag is in good condition, and I told him I like the patch on it. I am writing so you know where the requests at home may be coming from. Perhaps ask him what he would like about the new bag, not just who has it.

Kishore, Class 4B

qa.q: How many children came with the blue astronaut bag?
qa.a: About fifteen children.

qa.q: Why did Shankar keep his old bag under the desk?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and left out, because so many classmates had the new astronaut bag.

qa.q: What does Kishore suggest the parents try, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Shankar what he would like about the bag, not just who has it, so he can notice whether he wants it or just wants to match.

qa.q: How might Shankar's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel relieved to understand where his requests are coming from and better able to talk with him calmly.

grounding: A child wants the bag everyone in class has, less from liking it than from the sense that so many cannot be wrong.

passage: It was nearly eleven when the group stopped at a petrol pump on Bengaluru's ring road. Uma had her brother's scooter, and someone said, 'Triple seat to the lake, no helmets, it's two minutes.' Everyone laughed as if it was normal. Keerthana felt her stomach tighten. There were only two helmets, and the road was dark. But Uma was already on, Nisha squeezed in behind her, and everyone else looked relaxed. Maybe I'm being a baby, Keerthana thought. She climbed on at the back, knees pressed against the number plate. At the first turn an auto swerved out of a lane, and Uma braked so hard they nearly tipped. Nobody laughed now. Keerthana got off, legs shaking. 'I'm walking,' she said, and called Amma, who came in ten minutes and drove them all home.

qa.q: How many helmets did the group have?
qa.a: Only two.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she climbed on at the back?
qa.a: Keerthana felt tense and uneasy, but doubted her own fear because everyone else seemed relaxed.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do earlier next time?
qa.a: She could trust the tight feeling in her stomach and say 'I'm walking' or call home before getting on, even if the others seem relaxed.

qa.q: How might Amma feel getting the late-night call?
qa.a: Amma is probably frightened and relieved at once, glad that Keerthana called and that they all got home safely.

grounding: A teenager goes along with a risky ride because the whole group seems comfortable, doubting her own unease until a near miss.

passage:
'Ball's on the roof again,' said Deepak. 'Asif, your turn. Up the pipe.'
'The pipe? It's three floors.'
'Everyone's done it. Rohit, Salim, even the captain of 9B.'
'I don't know, yaar.'
'Scared?' Someone laughed. The whole group leaned on the wall, bored and easy.
'No, just... is it safe?'
'We'd know if it wasn't. Nobody's fallen.'
Asif put a hand on the pipe. It was cold, and loose at the bracket. Everyone's so chill, he thought. Maybe it's just me.
'Asif! Down. Now.' Mr Kurian was striding across the ground.
Asif let go. His hands were shaking.
'That pipe is loose. Who else has climbed it?' Silence. 'Right. I'm reporting this to the principal today, the roof gets locked, and your parents get a call this evening.'

qa.q: Who did Deepak say had already climbed the pipe?
qa.a: Rohit, Salim and the captain of 9B.

qa.q: What does Asif's thought 'Maybe it's just me' show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he felt uneasy and scared but doubted his own judgment because the group seemed so relaxed.

qa.q: What protective steps did Mr Kurian take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: He called Asif down, said he would report it to the principal that day, lock the roof and call parents, which stops the dare before someone falls.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when Mr Kurian asks who else climbed?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt nervous and caught out, suddenly seeing the dare as dangerous rather than normal.

grounding: A teenager nearly follows a risky dare because the whole group seems comfortable, and doubts his own unease; a teacher steps in the same day.

passage: I still think about the July day our gang went to the old bridge over the river near Kolhapur. The water was brown and fast from the rains. Madhav said, 'Everybody jumps in monsoon. It's tradition.' Six of them went in one after another, whooping, and climbed out downstream. They all looked so easy about it. My chest was tight, and I kept thinking, maybe I'm the only coward here. So I jumped. The current grabbed me harder than I expected, and I swallowed water. A fisherman, Baburao kaka, hauled me into his boat by my shirt. He didn't shout. He walked all of us home that evening and told each of our parents what had happened. The next week the panchayat put up a fence. I'm Naveen, and the tight chest was right.

qa.q: Who pulled Naveen out of the water?
qa.a: A fisherman, Baburao kaka, hauled Naveen into his boat.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling before jumping?
qa.a: Naveen felt anxious, with a tight chest, but doubted that feeling and felt like the only coward because the others looked so easy.

qa.q: What could Naveen do the next time the group's calm hides a risk?
qa.a: Naveen could trust the tight chest and step back, or tell a trusted adult about the dare, instead of treating the group's ease as proof of safety.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the 'tradition' after that day?
qa.a: Madhav may feel shaken and guilty, since calling it tradition helped pull Naveen in, and the fence shows the adults saw it as dangerous.

grounding: A teenager joins a risky river jump because the group seems comfortable and doubts their own unease; an adult responds the same day.

passage: Swati, you're choosing your college hostel by stars on the phone? Sit, let your Tushar Mama tell you about Shimla, 1994. I was twenty, on my first trip with three friends. We were starving, and on the Mall there were two dhabas side by side. One had a queue out of the door. The other had an old man and empty tables. 'The crowded one,' I said. 'So many people can't be wrong.' We waited forty minutes in the cold. The food was lukewarm and salty. Only when we left did I see the tourist bus parked outside; the whole queue was one group. Next day we tried the empty place. The old man made us rajma so good that I still dream about it. Popularity told me where people were, beta. It didn't tell me what was good.

qa.q: How long did the friends wait in the queue?

qa.q: Why did Tushar choose the crowded dhaba?
qa.a: Tushar felt hungry and sure that a queue meant good food, trusting the crowd rather than checking.

qa.a: At the first glance at the two dhabas; Tushar could have asked why one was crowded, or looked inside the empty one, before joining the queue.

qa.q: How might the old man at the empty dhaba have seen the young men walking past?
qa.a: He was probably used to tourists judging by the queue next door, and may have felt quietly pleased when they came back the next day.

passage: The deadline for the scholarship form was midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Wasim had eleven minutes to pick an online certificate course to list on it. He sorted by rating. 'Fifty-two thousand people can't be wrong.' 'When was it made?' Wasim didn't answer; the page was loading. He submitted the form at 11:58 and flopped back, relieved. passage: On Saturday evening in Lajpat Nagar, the queue at the momo stall ran past the shoe shop. The stall next to it, with the same steaming baskets, had two customers. 'This one,' Pranav said, joining the long line. 'Look at the crowd. Must be the best in Delhi.' Aparna glanced at the quiet stall. The cook there was folding each momo by hand. 'Did you read anything about it?' 'Don't need to. Queue says it all.' Twenty-five minutes later they had a plate each. Pranav bit in. The filling was mostly cabbage, the chutney watery. He chewed slowly and kept smiling. 'Good, na?' Aparna noticed a college group in matching T-shirts filling half the queue, all laughing at a phone. She bought one plate from the quiet stall on the way out. It was better. She didn't say so.

qa.q: What was mostly in the filling of Pranav's momos?
qa.a: The filling was mostly cabbage.

qa.a: Pranav probably felt a little disappointed but didn't want to admit it, having been so sure the queue meant quality.

passage:
Mentoring note, analytics team, 12 March

This week half the team signed up for a weekend 'fast-track' certification, 18,000 per seat, because everyone in the chat said it guaranteed promotion. I watched Preeti handle it differently. She read the thread, then asked in our stand-up, 'Has anyone here actually been promoted after it, or are we all just following each other?' Nobody had. She then messaged one person outside the team, the senior manager in hiring, who owes the course nothing, and asked directly. The answer: the certificate is not considered in reviews. Preeti shared the reply with the team, politely, without mocking anyone. Two people cancelled. My next step: I will put the hiring manager's answer in the team handbook and suggest Preeti lead a short session on how to check claims like this.

Hemant, team lead

qa.q: How much did the weekend certification cost per seat?
qa.a: 18,000 per seat.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she asked her question at stand-up?
qa.a: Preeti seemed doubtful and cautious, unsure whether the team had real information or was just following each other.

qa.q: Which step of Preeti's approach is most worth copying?
qa.a: Asking one trusted source who has nothing to gain, the hiring manager, before joining, and then sharing the answer without mocking anyone.

qa.q: How might the colleagues who had signed up feel after Preeti shared the reply?
qa.a: They may feel a little embarrassed, but also grateful and relieved, since two of them could cancel before paying.

grounding: An adult asks whether the crowd has real information or is copying, and checks with one trusted, independent source before joining.

passage:
Tuesday night

The building group has gone mad about water. Since Sunday, forty-odd messages: 'Municipal water is poison now', 'Everyone on the fourth floor switched to the tanker company', 'Book fast before slots finish.' Mrs Kulkarni booked. The Reddys booked. Even Farhan's parents almost booked. I nearly did too; it's hard to sit still when everyone around you is moving. But I asked myself: does anyone here actually know something, or are we all just copying the fourth floor? Nobody had shared a test, only other people's messages. So I called Farhan's cousin, who works in the ward water lab and has no reason to sell anything. He said this month's tests were normal and that he'd send the report. I posted it in the group, with a line saying it's okay to double-check anything with the ward office directly. Three people replied 'thank you'.

Anand

qa.a: The report from the ward water lab, with a line saying it's okay to double-check with the ward office.

qa.q: How might the neighbours who replied 'thank you' have felt?
qa.a: They probably felt relieved and calmer, having real information instead of a chain of worried messages.

passage: The January fog lay so thick over the school ground that the old banyan by the wall looked like a grey giant. At morning assembly Kunal heard it for the first time: 'The banyan is haunted. A lady in white walks there.' By lunch, Lalit said the same thing, and so did two girls from 5A. By the last bell, the lady had long hair and walked backwards. Kunal hadn't believed it at breakfast. Now, every time someone told it, it felt a little more true. At the gate, the watchman laughed. 'That tree? I've sat under it every night for twelve years. Only crows.' passage: Darshan, you're scared of the pond behind the school because everyone says it's haunted? Let your Rashmi Pishi tell you about Durga Puja when I was ten. Every telling added something: a red sari, a smell of smoke, footsteps. I didn't believe it on the first day. By Navami I couldn't walk past without my heart thumping. On Dashami, my Baba took my hand and walked me right under that tree at dusk. Nothing. Just shiuli flowers falling. I asked him, 'Then why did everyone say it?' qa.a: Harsha sir seems puzzled and a little worried, sensing the class has changed towards him without knowing why.

'Did you hear about Mrs Menon?' Bhavna whispered in the library.
'The PT teacher? What about her?' said Sahil.

grounding: A young adult forwards an alarming health message because many others have, taking its frequency as proof.

passage:
Sunday, late

The family group exploded today. Sarika Mami posted a message saying a new virus in chicken had killed '1,000 people in one week' and that everyone must stop eating it. Nine forwards in an hour. Mummy was already calling the butcher to cancel. I felt my own stomach knot; it sounded so certain. But before forwarding, I did three things. I searched for the claim and found the original post: a blog with no name, from two years ago. I checked the state health department page: no such outbreak. And I asked myself how common this would be if it were real. A thousand deaths in a week would be on every news channel, not only in forwards. So I didn't forward it. I called Sarika Mami instead, gently, and read her the health department's page. She was quiet, then said, 'Then why did everyone send it?' Good question.

Nikita

qa.q: Where did Nikita find the original post?
qa.a: On a blog with no name, from two years ago.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel on first reading the message?
qa.a: Nikita felt anxious, with a knotted stomach, because the message sounded so certain.

qa.q: Which of Nikita's steps could anyone use with a scary forward?
qa.a: Tracing the original source, checking an official page, and asking how common the thing would really be before deciding not to forward.

qa.q: How might Sarika Mami feel after the call?
qa.a: Sarika Mami may feel embarrassed and confused, but also relieved, wondering why so many people shared it.

grounding: An adult traces a claim to its source, asks how common the thing really is, stops the chain and gently explains to a worried relative.
